### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:30:46

Session B is done and committed locally (4152bd6); I've sent you the verdict, the paper claims and the budget curve.

**Short answer to your question: there is no improvement on the base paper overall, but there is enough for a paper.**

**Compared with the MVFA paper** (round 1 recorded its numbers):

| | MVFA paper | Our best round 3 arm |
|---|---|---|
| Brain pixel AUROC | 90.27 | **92.63** (MIL+10 %); 92.42 (MIL+25 %); 91.48 (MIL+100 %) |
| Brain AUPRO | 65.35 (released checkpoint, measured in round 1) | **73.29** (MIL+10 %) |
| Liver pixel AUROC | 97.85 | 96.64 |
| RESC pixel AUROC | 92.05 | 88.88 |
| Image AUROC (Brain / Liver / RESC) | 78.6 / 76.2 / 83.3 | 56–68 / 60–68 / 71–74 |

- **Brain:** every arm that adds MIL to some masks beats the published model's localisation, even with less data, fewer epochs and no test-set selection (the paper's checkpoint had all three).
- **But the Brain result is post hoc and Brain-only,** so it can't be claimed as it stands.
- **Liver, RESC and image-level detection** all stay below the paper.

**What a new paper can stand on:**
1. **Headline, confirmed under the frozen rules:** plain MIL trained only on image labels keeps **97 %** of mask-supervised MVFA's localisation, at least 92 % on every target. It has held in all three rounds: 0.967, 0.930, then 0.969 on fresh seeds at 20 epochs. That's a label-efficiency story: masks are expensive, image labels are cheap.
2. **Practical recipe, a secondary result:** adding MIL on the datasets that have no masks costs nothing. MIL+100 % matches MVFA; it doesn't beat it under the rules. The label-budget curve backs this up: 10 % of the masks lifts mean retention from 0.97 to 1.03.
3. **Honest replication record:** two of round 2's wins (MIL beats MVFA on Brain; PU+100 % beats MVFA) and the 10 % budget hypothesis did not hold. Reporting them protects the headline from a cherry-picking objection.
4. **A side finding worth a paragraph:** training 4× longer made MVFA's target image AUROC worse (Brain 65.7 → 56.3), so model selection on the source datasets doesn't track the target.

**To turn the Brain lead into a real claim**, the cheapest step is a pre-registered follow-up: MIL+10 % vs MVFA on Brain, fresh seeds 8–12, with a 5/5 rule frozen beforehand. That's 10 runs, about 1.5 h on both GPUs. If it holds, you could claim that 10 % of the masks plus image labels beats full-mask MVFA and the published model on brain MRI.

**Still open:**
- **Gate G2:** your review of the report, the verdict and the paper claims. I'll log your reply verbatim.
- **`PAPER_PLAN.md` was never supplied.** So `paper_inputs/task4_r3/` follows round 1's layout, and the framing section in the paper claims is my suggestion.

#!/bin/bash
# Downloads MVFA data, zero-shot checkpoints and CLIP weights to the HDD.
# The HDD (NTFS/fuseblk) rejects chmod, which gdown needs, so each file is
# downloaded to a temp dir on the SSD, copied without permissions, then removed.
set -u
G=/home/f20241442/divyam-backup-imported/proj/.venv-task4/bin/gdown
R=/mnt/HDD1/divyam/task4
TMP=/home/f20241442/divyam-backup-imported/proj/.dl_tmp
mkdir -p "$TMP"

fetch() {  # fetch <gdrive-id> <dest-dir> <name>
  local id=$1 dest=$2 name=$3
  if [ -f "$dest/$name.done" ]; then echo "$name already done"; return 0; fi
  rm -f "$TMP/$name"
  if $G -q "$id" -O "$TMP/$name" && cat "$TMP/$name" > "$dest/$name" && [ "$(stat -c%s "$TMP/$name")" = "$(stat -c%s "$dest/$name")" ]; then
    touch "$dest/$name.done"; echo "$name ok $(du -h "$dest/$name" | cut -f1)"
  else
    echo "$name FAILED"
  fi
  rm -f "$TMP/$name"
}

cd $R/clip && [ -s ViT-L-14-336px.pt ] && echo "CLIP already done"

### 🧑 User · 2026-11-23 11:38:24

what have we done that we can write a paper over it

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:38:46

You have one solid result to headline a paper, one secondary result, and a replication record behind them. No arm improves on MVFA overall, so the paper is not "we beat the base paper". It is "image labels are nearly enough to train MVFA's localisation, and we checked that carefully".

## What we did (Task 4, rounds 1–3)

- **The question:** MVFA's segmentation adapters (the part that draws anomaly maps) learn only from pixel masks, which are expensive. Can they learn from image labels ("this image is abnormal"), and does the localisation carry over to an imaging modality never seen in training?
- **The method:** plain top-k multiple-instance learning (MIL). An image's score is the mean of its 3 most anomalous patches, trained against the image label. We also tested the LLM pipeline's (Task 3's) two top-ranked refinements: normal-bank-gated MIL and nnPU.
- **The protocol:**
  - **Leave-one-modality-out:** train on the other datasets and test on the unseen one (Brain MRI, Liver CT, retinal OCT).
  - **From scratch, with source-only checkpoint selection:** unlike the released checkpoints, nothing is selected on test data.
  - **Paired seeds and pre-registered rules:** the analysis code was frozen and hashed before the GPU runs.
- **Three rounds:** about 190 training runs. Every run is reported, including the ones that failed to support an idea.

## What a paper can claim

**1. Headline (confirmed): image labels alone keep about 97 % of mask-supervised localisation.**
- MIL with no masks keeps 0.969 of MVFA's pixel AUROC on unseen modalities (pixel AUROC rescaled so 50 = chance, 1.0 = MVFA's), and at least 0.92 on every target.
- It held three times under increasingly strict conditions:

| Round | Retention | Seeds | Epochs | Baseline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.967 | 1 | 5 | released checkpoint |
| 2 | 0.930 | 3 | 5 | re-run MVFA |
| 3 | 0.969 | 3 fresh | 20 | re-run MVFA |

**2. Practical recipe (secondary): add MIL on the datasets that have no masks.**
- MVFA's masks plus MIL on the mask-less datasets **matches** MVFA. It is ahead on Brain and RESC and within one point on Liver.
- The label-budget curve: with masks for only 10 % of abnormal images, mean retention rises from 0.97 to 1.03. From 25 % onward it is level with full masks.
- A mechanism check fits this: the share of selected patches that fall inside true lesions grows with the share of masks (0.45 → 0.66 → 0.71 → 0.78). So masks buy localisation precision, not detection.

**3. An honest replication record (reviewers like this).**
- Both of the LLM pipeline's top-ranked ideas were falsified or unsupported (gated MIL; nnPU with an estimated or fixed π).
- Two earlier apparent wins vanished at 4× the training on fresh seeds: "MIL beats MVFA on Brain" and "PU+100 % beats MVFA". A 10 %-mask "matches MVFA" hypothesis also failed, on Liver.
- Reporting these shows the headline wasn't cherry-picked.

**4. A methodological side finding.**
- Training longer improved MVFA on its source datasets but made its target image AUROC worse (Brain 65.7 → 56.3).
- So model selection on the source datasets doesn't track image-level detection on an unseen modality. That is worth a paragraph.

## Two ways to frame it

| Angle | Pitch | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Weak supervision (recommended)** | "Image Labels Are Nearly Enough: Weakly Supervised Adapters for Cross-Modality Medical Anomaly Localisation" | Medical imaging / MICCAI-style workshops |
| **B. Replicating AI-proposed research** | An LLM pipeline proposed the ideas; pre-registered replication kept 1 of 4 positive signals and falsified its top ideas | AI-for-science / reproducibility workshops |

A leads, and B's material becomes the "what did not hold" section and the disclosure. `PAPER_CLAIMS.md` already has three title options, the contribution sentence, the main table, the figure list and the limitations.

## What reviewers will push on

- **No overall improvement on MVFA.** Liver, RESC and image AUROC are all below the published model.
- **Image-level detection is weak for every arm** under source-only selection. Brain image AUROC is near chance for the re-run MVFA.
- **A reduced setup:** 20 epochs (MVFA uses 50), at most 1,000 images per dataset, 3 seeds, one codebase.
- **The best Brain numbers are post hoc.** MIL+10 % reaches 92.6 pixel AUROC against the paper's 90.3, and 73.3 AUPRO against 59.3 for the re-run MVFA. This is the most eye-catching number, and it can't be claimed yet.

## What would make it stronger (optional, outside the plan)

1. **A pre-registered Brain follow-up:** MIL+10 % vs MVFA on fresh seeds 8–12, with the 5/5 rule frozen beforehand. About 1.5 h of GPU. If it holds, you'd have a real positive: "10 % of the masks plus image labels beats full-mask MVFA and the published model on brain MRI."
2. **Log target image AUROC per epoch,** for analysis only (never for selection), to explain why longer training hurts it.

Everything the paper needs is in `task4r3/report/paper_inputs/task4_r3/` and in the zip you have.

### 🧑 User · 2026-11-23 11:39:13

in simple and short?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:39:18

**What we did:** we trained MVFA's anomaly-map part using only image labels ("abnormal or not") instead of pixel masks. Then we tested it on a scan type it had never seen. We ran this over 3 rounds, with the rules fixed in advance.

**What we can claim in a paper:**
1. **Main result:** image labels alone get about 97 % of the localisation quality you get with full masks. This held in all 3 rounds.
2. **Practical tip:** adding image-label training on the datasets that have no masks costs nothing, and the model still matches MVFA. With masks for only 10 % of the abnormal images, you get about full-mask quality on average.
3. **Honest negatives:** the two AI-suggested improvements failed, and two earlier "wins" disappeared when we re-checked them.

**What we can't claim:** that we beat the MVFA paper. We beat it only on Brain (92.6 vs 90.3 pixel AUROC), and that wasn't a pre-planned test.

**To strengthen it:** one extra 1.5-hour GPU run on Brain, with the rules fixed in advance, could turn that Brain result into a real claim.

### 🧑 User · 2026-11-23 11:39:50

so basically we are getting similar results but with less expensive training?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:39:55

Almost, but the saving is in **labelling, not training**.

- **Training cost is about the same.** The same model trains for the same number of epochs, so the GPU time doesn't change.
- **Labelling is what gets much cheaper.** MVFA needs pixel masks, where a doctor outlines every lesion. Our MIL only needs a yes/no per image ("abnormal or not"), which is far cheaper to collect.

So the pitch is **nearly the same localisation (about 97 %) with far cheaper labels.** With a small number of masks (10 %) on top, it reaches about full-mask quality on average.

One caveat: "similar" holds on Brain and Liver. On the retina (RESC) it is a bit lower without masks (92 % retention).

### 🧑 User · 2026-11-23 11:40:22

how did we come up with this

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:40:29

It came out of the earlier tasks, partly by accident.

1. **Task 3 (the AI idea pipeline)** posed the problem: can MVFA's map-drawing part learn from image labels instead of masks? Plain MIL was the basic experiment, and the pipeline ranked a few "smarter" versions on top of it.
2. **Round 1** tested one of those versions (a PU loss). It didn't help, but the plain MIL baseline we ran next to it surprised us: it kept about 97 % of MVFA's localisation without any masks.
3. **Round 2** tested the pipeline's top-ranked idea (gated MIL) and a fixed version of PU. Both failed. Plain MIL held up again (93 %).
4. **Round 3** checked it properly: 4× longer training, fresh seeds, rules fixed in advance. It held (97 %). Two other earlier "wins" disappeared. We also tried mixing MIL with a few masks, which gives the "10 % of masks" result.

So we didn't set out to prove "image labels are enough". The simple baseline kept winning while the clever ideas failed, and round 3 confirmed it.

### 🧑 User · 2026-11-23 11:41:00

so task 3 suggested we do this?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:41:06

Partly.

**What Task 3 suggested:**
- **The question:** can MVFA learn localisation from image labels instead of masks? (Problem A1.)
- **Plain MIL as the main experiment** for answering it.
- **Two side analyses** that we ran in round 3: adding the image-label loss on datasets without masks (MIL+100 %), and trying small mask budgets (10 % / 25 %).
- **"Smarter" improvements on plain MIL,** ranked by the pipeline: gated MIL first, adaptive-k MIL third (which round 1 refined into PU).

**What Task 3 got wrong:** its top-ranked improvements failed. Gated MIL was worse than plain MIL, and PU didn't help.

**What came from our testing:** the finding that the plain baseline itself is the result. It nearly matches masks, and it held over 3 rounds.

So Task 3 gave us the question and the experiments. The answer, and the finding that its own "best ideas" didn't help, came from the runs.

### 🧑 User · 2026-11-23 11:42:00

our are results worse than the base paper or near it ?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:42:06

**For localisation (the maps), we're near it. For detection (is the image abnormal?), we're clearly worse.**

| | MVFA paper | Our MIL (no masks) | Our best arm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brain map quality (pixel AUROC) | 90.3 | 88.6 (near) | **92.6 (better)** |
| Liver map quality | 97.9 | 95.5 (near) | 96.6 (near) |
| Retina (RESC) map quality | 92.1 | 83.4 (worse) | 88.9 (a bit worse) |
| Detection (image AUROC) | 76–83 | 67–71 | 68–73 (worse) |

Our setup was handicapped compared with the paper:
- less data: at most 1,000 images per dataset;
- shorter training: 20 epochs vs 50;
- no picking of the best checkpoint using test data, which the paper's checkpoint had.

Even our own re-run of MVFA, with masks, scores below the paper under these conditions. So the fair comparison is ours against ours: MIL vs our MVFA re-run. That's where the 97 % comes from.

### 🧑 User · 2026-11-23 11:42:41

so is it worth writing a paper on this?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-23 11:42:46

**Yes, for a workshop paper. Not for a main conference as it stands.**

**Why it's worth writing:**
- The main result is clear, useful and well tested: cheap image labels give about 97 % of mask-quality localisation, and it held over 3 rounds with rules fixed in advance.
- Saving annotation cost is a real concern in medical imaging, so people care about this.
- The careful process (fixed rules, every run reported, the failed ideas included) makes it credible.

**Why not a main conference yet:**
- We don't beat the base paper, and detection is clearly worse.
- The setup is reduced: less data, shorter training, 3 seeds.
- The most exciting number (the Brain result) wasn't a pre-planned test.

**To make it stronger, cheaply:** run the 1.5-hour Brain follow-up. If 10 % of the masks still beats MVFA there, you'd have a real "better than the base paper" result to lead with.

My advice: write it for a medical-imaging workshop now. Add the Brain run if you can book the GPUs once more.

 "content": "# Follow-up rule (frozen before any follow-up run)\n\n**Why this run exists.** In round 3, MIL with masks for 10 % of the masked sources' abnormal images (`mil_m10`) was ahead of the re-run MVFA on Brain AUPRO on every seed (3–5), by 10.9–16.3 points. Its Brain pixel AUROC (92.63) was also above the MVFA paper's (90.27). Both were **post-hoc** observations (round 3 report §4, VERDICT weakness 3, ISSUES_LOG G3-5), so neither could be claimed. This follow-up tests the Brain effect once, under a rule fixed in advance, on seeds that have never been used.\n\n**Runs.** 10 runs: `mvfa` and `mil_m10` on the Brain fold, seeds **8, 9, 10, 11, 12**, 20 epochs. They use round 3's code, data subsample, source-validation checkpointing and evaluation, all unchanged (`task4fu/README.md`). Seeds 3–7 are never pooled with them.\n\n## The one pre-registered test (FU-H)\n\n**FU-H: MIL+10 % beats MVFA on Brain.** For each seed s, Δ_AUPRO(s) = AUPRO(mil_m10, s) − AUPRO(mvfa, s) on the Brain test set; Δ_pix(s) is defined the same way for pixel AUROC.\n\n| Outcome | Condition |\n|---|---|\n| **CONFIRMED** | Δ_AUPRO > 0 on **5 of 5** seeds (one-sided sign test p = 0.031 ≤ 0.05; one test, so no correction) **and** mean Δ_pix > 0 |\n| **holds on most seeds (not confirmed)** | Δ_AUPRO > 0 on 4 of 5 seeds |\n| **did not replicate** | Δ_AUPRO > 0 on 3 or fewer of 5 seeds, **or** 5/5 with mean Δ_pix ≤ 0 |\n| **incomplete** | Fewer than 5 seed pairs have both runs. The result is reported as \"k/n pairs\", and CONFIRMED cannot be reached |\n\n- Ties (Δ = 0) count against MIL+10 %, as in rounds 2–3.\n- Points = AUROC/AUPRO × 100, read from `results/results.csv`, rows not marked SMOKE.\n- Only `evaluate_target.py` reads the Brain test set, after selection on source validation.\n\n## Descriptive (reported, not tested)\n\n- Image AUROC: per-seed and mean Δ (MIL+10 % − MVFA). Round 3 found MVFA's Brain image AUROC near chance at 20 epochs.\n- MIL+10 % Brain pixel AUROC against the **MVFA paper's 90.27**: on how many seeds it is above, and the mean.         assert {k for k, d, p, y in items if p not in s} == {"weak"}
    assert s10 == mask_budget_set("mil_m10", fold, seed, L)          # fixed for the seed

        assert got == ref, arm

GPU smoke test: both arms, 50 steps, Brain fold, seed 8 (stops on failure; never recorded)\n#   4. ./run_all.sh fu: the 10 runs (5 per GPU, all at once, about 1-1.5 h); finished runs are skipped on a restart\n#   5. analyze_fu.py -> results/analysis_fu.md (the outcome is printed in logs/stage.txt)\n# Restart after an interruption: tmux new -d -s fu './go.sh launch'\nset -u\ncd \"$(dirname \"$0\")\"\nPY=/home/f20241442/divyam-backup-imported/proj/.venv-task4/bin/python\nexport GPUS=${GPUS:-0 1}\nMIN_FREE_MB=${MIN_FREE_MB:-45000} MAX_UTIL=${MAX_UTIL:-20} POLL=${POLL:-300}\nHDD=${TASK4R3_HDD:-/mnt/HDD1/divyam/task4/fu}\nmkdir -p logs\nstage() { echo \"$(date '+%F %T') $*\" | tee -a logs/stage.txt; }\n\nfrozen_ok() { [ -f report/FROZEN.sha256 ] && sha256sum -c --quiet report/FROZEN.sha256; }\n\ngpus_free() {\n  local ok=1\n  for g in $GPUS; do\n    read -r free util < <(nvidia-smi -i \"$g\" --query-gpu=memory.free,utilization.gpu --format=csv,noheader,nounits | tr -d ',')\n    echo \"  gpu $g: ${free} MiB free, ${util} % load\"\n    { [ \"$free\" -ge \"$MIN_FREE_MB\" ] && [ \"$util\" -le \"$MAX_UTIL\" ]; } || ok=0\n  done\n  [ $ok = 1 ]\n}\n\nwait_for_gpus() {\n  [ \"${FORCE:-0}\" = 1 ] && { stage \"FORCE=1: not waiting for free GPUs\"; return; }\n  stage \"waiting for free GPUs ($GPUS; need >= $MIN_FREE_MB MiB free and <= $MAX_UTIL % load, 3 checks in a row)\"\n  local n=0\n  while [ $n -lt 3 ]; do\n    if gpus_free; then n=$((n + 1)); else n=0; fi\n    [ $n -lt 3 ] && sleep $([ $n = 0 ] && echo \"$POLL\" || echo 60)\n  done\n  stage \"GPUs free\"\n}\n\nlaunch() {\n  frozen_ok || { stage \"STOPPED: rules not frozen or changed (report/FROZEN.sha256)\"; exit 1; }\n  stage \"follow-up runs started ($(./run_all.sh list | wc -l) runs in the plan)\"\n  ./run_all.sh fu >> logs/fu_console.log 2>&1\n  stage \"follow-up runs finished; $(grep -c 'FAILED TWICE' logs/fu_console.log) failed twice\"\n  if $PY analyze_fu.py > logs/analyze_fu.log 2>&1; then stage \"$(tail -1 logs/analyze_fu.log)\"\n  else stage \"analyze_fu.py failed (logs/analyze_fu.log)\"; fi\n  stage \"DONE. Results: results/analysis_fu.md. Next: Claude writes report/FU_REPORT.md (task4fu/STATE.md)\"\n}\n\ncase \"${1:-all}\" in\n  launch) launch; exit ;;\n  all) ;;\n  *) sed -n 2,13p \"$0\"; exit 1 ;;\nesac\n\nCUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=\"\" $PY -m pytest -q -p no:anyio tests/ > logs/pytest_prelaunch.log 2>&1 || { stage \"STOPPED: tests fail (logs/pytest_prelaunch.log)\"; exit 1; }\nstage \"tests pass ($(tail -1 logs/pytest_prelaunch.log))\"\nfrozen_ok || { stage \"STOPPED: rules not frozen or changed (report/FROZEN.sha256)\"; exit 1; }\nwait_for_gpus\n\nstage \"GPU smoke test (2 arms x 50 steps)\"\n./run_all.sh smoke > logs/smoke_console.log 2>&1\nok=1\nfor a in mvfa mil_m10; do\n  [ -f \"$HDD/smoke_runs/${a}_Brain_s8/run.json\" ] || ok=0\ndone\ngrep -q \"FAILED\" logs/smoke_console.log && ok=0\n[ -f results/results.csv ] && grep -q \"SMOKE\\|_s8,.*,1,.*max_steps\" results/results.csv && ok=0\n[ $ok = 1 ] || { stage \"STOPPED: smoke test FAILED (logs/smoke_console.log, logs/train2.py_*max_steps*.log)\"; exit 1; }\nstage \"smoke test PASS (both arms ran 50 steps and wrote run.json; nothing recorded in results.csv)\"\n\nlaunch\n"

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-24 15:13:30

They're harmless, and they're our own processes, not anyone else's.

**What they are:** each of the 5 runs on GPU 1 also opens an idle CUDA context, about 550 MB, on GPU 0. The cause is `pin_memory=True` in the data loader (`train2.py:283`). PyTorch's pin-memory thread starts CUDA on the default device, which is `cuda:0`, because the code never calls `torch.cuda.set_device`. The context holds memory but does no compute; all of those runs' real work is on GPU 1.

**Cost:** 5 × 550 MB ≈ 2.75 GB on a 97 GB card, with no effect on speed or results. Round 3 ran the same code, so its GPU‑1 runs did the same thing.

**Not fixing it now:** `train2.py` has to stay byte-identical to round 3; a test checks this. Changing it would also mean killing the 10 runs that are going. I'll log it as FU‑5 in the write-up.

If someone else needs GPU 0 memory later, the fix for a future round is to run each GPU‑1 job with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1` and `--device cuda:0`. For now, the runs continue.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-24 16:09:50

The pre-registered test came back **CONFIRMED**: with masks for only 10 % of the abnormal source images plus image labels for the rest, the model localises lesions on unseen brain MRI better than full-mask MVFA. All 10 runs finished between 20:37 and 21:38 with no failures. The GPUs are free again.

| Brain, seeds 8–12 | pixel AUROC | AUPRO | image AUROC |
|---|---|---|---|
| MVFA (re-run, full masks) | 87.00 | 57.38 | 63.29 |
| **MIL+10 %** | **92.36** | **72.08** | 64.37 |

- **The pre-registered test:** AUPRO was higher with MIL+10 % on all 5 seeds, by 12.5 to 19.1 points (p = 0.031). Pixel AUROC was higher on every seed too, by 5.35 on average. Under the rule we froze before the run, that counts as CONFIRMED.
- **It repeats round 3:** the new seeds land within about 1 point of round 3's seeds 3–5 (92.63 pixel AUROC / 73.29 AUPRO).
- **Against the published MVFA, for context only:** MIL+10 % was above the paper's Brain pixel AUROC of 90.27 on all 5 seeds (mean +2.1). It was above round 1's AUPRO for the released checkpoint (65.35) on all 5 too (mean +6.7). The training setups differ, so this can't be written as "beats MVFA".
- **Limits to state in the paper:**
  - The result is Brain only. On Liver, MIL+10 % still trails MVFA (round 3), and RESC was not tested.
  - Image-level detection did not improve (+1.08 on average, lower on 2 of 5 seeds).
  - Why it happens is untested.

For the paper, this means it can lead with two confirmed results: image labels nearly match masks on every target (H1, from round 3), and 10 % masks plus image labels beat full masks on Brain.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-11-21 17:30:36

**All the Task 4 runs should take about 2–3 GPU-hours, or about 1.5 hours if both cards are free.** That's lower than my earlier 3–4 hours, now that I've read MVFA's training code. It's still an estimate from the code, not a timing; Step 2's 50-step dry run will give the real number in about 10 minutes.

**Why it's fast:** every training step is one image at 240 px through ViT-L/14 (the PU step uses a pair), in mixed precision, with gradients only through the adapters and the upper layers. With one image per step, the GPU spends most of its time launching small kernels rather than computing. On an RTX PRO 6000 I expect about 30–60 ms per step, so a 2,000-step fine-tune takes 2–3 minutes.

| Item | Count | GPU time each | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Timing dry run (Step 2) | 1 | ~10 min | 10 min |
| R0 evaluation (Liver, Brain, RESC) | 3 | ~1–2 min | ~5 min |
| π estimation (segmentation and detection branch) | 6 | < 1 min | ~5 min |
| M-h + M-h-ctrl fine-tune and evaluation | 18 | ~3–4 min | ~1–1.2 h |
| M + B0 training and evaluation | 8 | ~3–4 min | ~0.5 h |
| Optional: M at 2S, λ = 0.5 | 2 | ~4–6 min | ~10 min |
| **Total** | | | **≈ 2–2.5 h, ≈ 3 h with buffer** |

If the early-stop rule applies after Liver, about 20 minutes less.

**Ways to use less of other people's time:**
- **Run several jobs per GPU.** Each run needs only about 5 GB of memory, and one-image steps leave the card mostly idle. On a free 96 GB card, 3–4 jobs at once should take total time down to roughly 45–60 minutes on both cards.
- **Compute AUPRO on CPU after the GPU part finishes.** It's the slowest part of evaluation, especially for Brain with about 3,700 test images, and it doesn't need the GPU. A job can save its anomaly maps, free the GPU, and score them afterwards.
- **Split it into two short GPU sessions if that's easier to arrange:**
  1. About 20 minutes for the dry run, R0 and π. This catches setup problems early.
  2. About 1–2 hours for all the training runs.

**A download problem in the original session:** the download script is still running and copying files to the HDD. But `cp` fails when it tries to set permissions on the HDD, so the script labels every file FAILED and never marks it done. The data itself looks intact: Liver's file has exactly the same size as in the first attempt. The fix is to copy with `cat src > dest` instead of `cp`, then check each archive with `tar -tzf`.
